grab.e: From Middle Dutch grabben or Middle Low German grabben (“to grasp, grab, seize, snatch”), from Old Saxon gravan, from Proto-West Germanic *grabbōn, a secondary form of Proto-Germanic *grabōną (“to gather, rake”), from Proto-Indo-European *gʰrebʰ- (“to gather, rake, grab, seize”).
grab.g: To grip suddenly; to seize; to clutch.

grab.e: From Arabic غُرَاب (ḡurāb) and Hindi ghurb?: crow, raven, a kind of Arab ship.
grab.g: A two- or three-masted vessel used on the Malabar coast.

grace.e: From Middle English grace, from Old French grace (modern French grâce), from Latin grātia (“kindness, favour, esteem”), from grātus (“pleasing”), from Proto-Indo-European *gʷerH- (“to praise, welcome”); compare grateful.

graceful.e: From Middle English graceful. By surface analysis, grace + -ful.
graceful.g: Having or showing grace in movement, shape, or proportion.

gracious.e: From Middle English gracious, from Old French gracieus, from Latin gratiosus, from gratia (“esteem, favor”).
gracious.g: Of, related to, full of, or exhibiting grace.

graciously.e: From Middle English graciously, graciousliche; equivalent to gracious + -ly.
graciously.g: In a gracious manner; with grace and courtesy.

graft.e: From Middle English graffe, from Old French greffe (“stylus”), from Latin graphium (“stylus”), from Ancient Greek γραφείον (grapheíon), from γράφειν (gráphein, “to write”); probably akin to English carve. So named from the resemblance of a scion or shoot to a pointed pencil.
graft.g: A small shoot or scion of a tree inserted in another tree, the stock of which is to support and nourish it. The two unite and become one tre

graft.e: From Middle Dutch graft (“canal”), from graven (“dig”). The contemporary senses “depth of digging blade” and “narrow spade” may have a separate history, but this is uncertain.

grain.e: From Middle English greyn, grayn, grein, from Old French grain, grein, from Latin grānum (“seed”), from Proto-Indo-European *ǵr̥h₂nóm (“grain”).
grain.g: The harvested seeds of various grass food crops, especially wheat, maize, rye, barley, and rice.

grain.e: From Middle English grayn, from Old Norse grein (“bough, branch”), from Proto-Germanic *grainiz (“branch, twig, ramification”), of unknown origin.
grain.g: A branch of a tree; a stalk or stem of a plant; an offshoot.

granary.e: Borrowed from Latin grānārium (16th century). Equivalent to grain + -ary.
granary.g: A storage facility for grain or sometimes animal feed.

grandfather.e: From grandfather clause: see grandfather (etymology 1) and clause.
grandfather.g: To retain discontinued laws or rules for (an object, individual or organization previously affected by them).

grandmother.e: From Middle English graundmodre, grauntmoder, granmoder; equivalent to grand- + mother. Superseded earlier eldmother, eldermother.

grant.e: From Middle English granten, graunten, grantien, grauntien, from Anglo-Norman granter, graunter, from Old French granter, graunter, graanter, greanter (“to promise, assure, guarantee, confirm, ratify”).

grape.e: From Middle English grape, borrowed from Old French grappe (“cluster of fruit or flowers, bunch of grapes”), deverbal from graper (“to pick grapes”, literally “to hook”), borrowed from Frankish *krappō (“to hook”), from Proto-Indo-European *greb- (“hook”) or *gremb- (“crooked, uneven”).
grape.g: A small, round, smooth-skinned edible fruit, usually purple, red, or green, that grows in bunches on female vines of most species of genus V

grapevine.g: The plant, a vine of genus Vitis, on which grapes grow.

grasp.e: From Middle English graspen, grapsen, craspen (“to grope; feel around”), from Old English *grǣpsian, from Proto-West Germanic *graipisōn, from Proto-Germanic *graipisōną, from Proto-Indo-European *gʰrebʰ- (“to take, seize, rake”), the same ultimate source as grab.
grasp.g: To grip; to take hold, particularly with the hand.

grass.e: From Middle English gras, from Old English græs, from Proto-West Germanic *gras, from Proto-Germanic *grasą (“grass”), from Proto-Indo-European *gʰreh₁- (“to grow”). The "informer" sense is probably a shortening of grasshopper (“police officer, informant”), rhyming slang for copper (“police officer”) or shopper (“informant”).
grass.g: Any plant of the family Poaceae, characterized by leaves that arise from nodes in the stem and leaf bases that wrap around the stem, especia

grasshopper.e: From Middle English grashoppere, alteration of earlier grashoppe, from Old English græshoppa (“grasshopper”). Equivalent to grass + hopper.
grasshopper.g: A mostly herbivorous insect of the order Orthoptera, noted for its ability to jump long distances and for the habit of some species communic

grate.e: From Middle English grate, from a Medieval Latin crāta, from a Latin word for a hurdle; or Italian grata, from Latin cratis.
grate.g: A horizontal metal grill through which liquid, ash, or small objects can fall, while larger objects cannot.

grateful.e: From grate (“(obsolete) serving to gratify, agreeable, pleasing; grateful, thankful”) + -ful (suffix forming adjectives with the sense of tending to have or thoroughly having a quality). Grate is a learned borrowing from Latin grātus (“agreeable, pleasing; beloved, dear.
grateful.g: Of a person or their actions, feelings, etc.: expressing gratitude or appreciation; appreciative, thankful.

gratify.e: From French gratifier, from Latin grātificō (“to do a favor to, oblige, please, gratify”), from grātus (“kind, pleasing”) + faciō (“to make”).

gratitude.e: From French gratitude, from Medieval Latin grātitūdō (“thankfulness”), from Latin grātus (“thankful”).

grave.e: From Middle English grave, grafe, from Old English græf, grafu (“cave, grave, trench”), from Proto-West Germanic *grab, from Proto-Germanic *grabą, *grabō (“grave, trench, ditch”), from Proto-Indo-European *gʰrebʰ- (“to dig, scratch, scrape”).
grave.g: An excavation in the earth as a place of burial.

grave.e: From Middle English graven, from Old English grafan (“to dig, dig up, grave, engrave, carve, chisel”), from Proto-Germanic *grabaną (“to dig”), from Proto-Indo-European *gʰrebʰ- (“to dig, scratch, scrape”).

graveclothes.g: The clothes in which a corpse is buried.

gravedigger.g: A person employed to dig graves.

gravel.e: From Middle English gravel, grauel, from Old French gravele, diminutive of grave (“gravel, seashore”), from Medieval Latin grava, ultimately from Proto-Celtic *grāwā (“gravel, pebbles”) (compare Breton groa, Cornish grow, Welsh gro), from Proto-Indo-European *gʰroh₁weh₂, from *gʰreh₁w- (“to grind”).
gravel.g: Small fragments of rock, used for laying on the beds of roads and railways, and as ballast.

graven.e: From Middle English graven, igraven, from Old English grafen, ġegrafen, from Proto-Germanic *grabanaz, past participle of Proto-Germanic *grabaną (“to dig, trench”).

gravity.e: Borrowed from French gravité (“seriousness, solemnity; severity; (physics) gravity”), or from its etymon Latin gravitās (“heaviness, weight; seriousness; severity”), equivalent to grave (“serious”) + -ity (suffix forming nouns, especially abstract nouns). Gravitās is derived from gravis (“heavy.

gray.e: From Middle English gray, from Old English grǣġ (West Saxon). The spelling gray reflects the West Saxon vowel development, whereas the variant grey stems from the Anglian form grēġ (through Middle English grey). Further derived from Proto-West Germanic *grāu, from Proto-Germanic *grēwaz (“grey”), from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰreh₁- (“to green, to grow”).
gray.g: Of a color between black and white, having neutral hue and intermediate brightness.

graze.e: From Middle English grasen (“to feed with grass”), from Old English grasian, from Proto-West Germanic *grasōn, from Proto-Germanic *grasōną, from *grasą (“grass”) + *-ōną (verbal suffix).
graze.g: The act of grazing; a scratching or injuring lightly on passing.

grease.e: From Middle English grece, from Anglo-Norman grece, from Vulgar Latin *crassia, noun derived from Latin crassus (“fat, thick”).
grease.g: Animal fat in a melted or soft state.

great.e: From Middle English greet, grete (“great, large”), from Old English grēat (“big, massive; tall; thick; coarse”), from Proto-West Germanic *graut, from Proto-Germanic *grautaz (“coarse, crude; big, large”), from Proto-Indo-European *gʰrewd-, *gʰer- (“to rub; to stroke; to grind; to remove”).
great.g: Taking up a lot of space; large.

greatly.e: From Middle English gretly. By surface analysis, great + -ly.
greatly.g: To a great extent or degree.

greatness.e: From Middle English gretnesse, gretnes, greetnesse, from Old English grēatnes. Equivalent to great + -ness.
greatness.g: The state, condition, or quality of being great

greaves.e: From Low German (compare German Low German Greev, Greve (“greaves”)), from Middle Low German grêve, from Old Saxon *griovo, from Proto-West Germanic *greubō (“roughage, brushwood, kindling”), perhaps related to *grubaz (“rough, coarse”), the root of German Griebe (“greaves, crackling”). Possibly related to gruff.
greaves.g: The unmeltable residue left after animal fat has been rendered.

greed.g: A selfish or excessive desire for more than is needed or deserved, especially of money, wealth, food, or other possessions.

greedily.e: From Middle English gredyly, gredily, from Old English grǣdiglīce, grǣdelīce; equivalent to greedy + -ly.
greedily.g: In a greedy manner; with keen or ardent desire.

greediness.e: From Middle English gredynesse, from Old English grǣdiġnes; equivalent to greedy + -ness.
greediness.g: The state of being greedy; greed.

greedy.e: From Middle English gredy, from Anglian Old English grēdiġ (“greedy, hungry, eager”) (cognate West Saxon form grǣdiġ), from Proto-Germanic *grēdagaz (“hungry”), from Proto-Germanic *grēdaz, *grēduz, *grēdô (“hunger”), from Proto-Indo-European *gʰer-. Equivalent to greed + -y. Sanskrit गृद्धि (gṛddhi, “greed”) is a false cognate.
greedy.g: Having greed; consumed by selfish desires.

green.e: From Middle English grene, from Old English grēne, from Proto-West Germanic *grōnī, from Proto-Germanic *grōniz, from Proto-Indo-European *gʰreh₁- (“to grow”). The sense of obscene, pornographic, or sexual in the Philippines is a semantic loan from Spanish verde.
green.g: The color of grass and leaves; a primary additive color midway between yellow and blue which is evoked by light between roughly 495–570 nm.

green.e: From Middle English grenen, from Old English grēnian (“to become green, flourish”), from Proto-West Germanic *grōnijan, from Proto-Germanic *grōnijōną, *grōnijaną (“to become green”), from the adjective (see above).
green.g: To make or turn (something) green or greener.

greenish.e: From Middle English grenisch, grenysch, equivalent to green + -ish.

greenness.e: From Middle English grennesse, from Old English grennes; equivalent to green + -ness.
greenness.g: The state or quality of being green; green colour.

greet.e: From Middle English greten, from Old English grētan, from Proto-West Germanic *grōtijan, from Proto-Germanic *grōtijaną.
greet.g: To welcome in a friendly manner, either in person or through another means such as writing.

greet.e: From a blend of two Old English verbs, grētan, grǣtan (itself from Proto-West Germanic *grātan); and of Old English grēotan (itself from *greutan), both meaning "to weep, lament". Possibly reinforced in Northern England and Scotland by Old Norse gráta, whence also Danish græde, Norwegian gråte, Swedish gråta, all meaning "to cry, to weep".

greeting.g: A conventional phrase used to start a letter or conversation or otherwise to acknowledge a person's arrival or presence.

greyhound.e: From Old English grīġhund, from a cognate or borrowing of Old Norse grøy (“bitch”) (whence Icelandic grey, thus not related to the colour grey) plus hund (“hound”). Altered by folk etymology to appear to be grey + hound and so in the form grayhound by analogy.
greyhound.g: A lean breed of dog used in hunting and racing.

griddle.e: From Middle English gridil, from Anglo-Norman gredil, variant of Old French greil, from Latin crāticulum, diminutive of crātis.
griddle.g: A stone or metal flat plate or surface on which food is fried or baked.

grief.e: From Middle English greef, gref, from Old French grief (“grave, heavy, grievous, sad”), from Latin gravis (“heavy, grievous, sad”).

grievance.e: From Old French grievance, from the verb grever (“to irritate; to bother; to annoy”) + -ance, equivalent to grieve + -ance.

grieve.e: From Middle English greven, from Old French grever (“to burden”), from Latin gravō, gravāre, from adjective gravis (“grave”). For the meaning development compare Russian тяготи́ть (tjagotítʹ, “to be a burden (on), to oppress”), Russian тужи́ть (tužítʹ, “to experience grief”), related to тяжёлый (tjažólyj, “heavy, grave”), тя́жкий (tjážkij).
grieve.g: To cause sorrow or distress to.

grieve.e: From Middle English greve, greyve, grave, grafe, from Old Norse greifi, from Middle Low German grēve, grâve, related to Old English grœfa, groefa, variants of Old English ġerēfa (“steward, reeve”).
grieve.g: A governor of a town or province.

grievous.e: From Middle English grevous, from Anglo-Norman grevous, from Old French grever, from Latin gravō (“to burden”). Developed in the 13th century. Equivalent to grief + -ous.

grievously.e: From Middle English grevously; equivalent to grievous + -ly.

grievousness.g: the quality or state of being grievous

grind.e: From Middle English grynden, from Old English grindan (“to grind”), from Proto-West Germanic *grindan, from Proto-Germanic *grindaną (“to crush, grind”).
grind.g: To reduce to smaller pieces by crushing with lateral motion.
A traditional communal pilot whale hunt in the Faroe Islands.

grinder.e: From Middle English grinder, grindere, from Old English grindere (“one or that which grinds; grinder”), equivalent to grind + -er.
grinder.g: One who grinds something, such as the teeth.

grinding.e: From Middle English gryndynge. By surface analysis, grind + -ing.
grinding.g: The action of grinding together or crushing into small particles; the sound of this action.

grip.e: Verb from Middle English grippen, from Old English grippan, from a Proto-Germanic *gripjaną (compare Old High German gripfen); compare the related Old English grīpan, whence English gripe.
grip.g: To take hold (of), particularly with the hand.

grip.e: From Middle English grip, grippe, gryppe (“a ditch, drain”), from Old English grēp (“a furrow, burrow”) and grēpe (“a furrow, ditch, drain”), from Proto-Germanic *grōpiz (“a furrow, groove”). Related also to Old English grōp (“a ditch, drain”).
grip.g: A small ditch or trench; a channel to carry off water or other liquid; a drain.

groan.e: From Middle English gronen, granen, from Old English grānian (“to groan; lament; murmur”), from Proto-West Germanic *grainōn, from Proto-Germanic *grainōną (“to howl; weep”), from Proto-Germanic *grīnaną (“to whine; howl; whimper”).
groan.g: A low, mournful sound uttered in pain or grief.

groaning.e: From Middle English gronynge (“groaning”), from Old English grānung; equivalent to groan + -ing. Conflated with Middle English gronende, present participle of gronen, from Old English grāniende, present participle of grānian (“to groan”). Analyzable as groan + -ing.

grope.e: From Middle English gropien, from Old English grāpian, related to grīpan (whence English gripe); compare also grip.
grope.g: To feel with or use the hands; to handle.

gross.e: From Middle English gros (“large, thick, full-bodied; coarse, unrefined, simple”), from Old French gros, from Latin grossus (“big, fat, thick”, in Late Latin also “coarse, rough”), of uncertain further origin but perhaps related to Proto-Celtic *brassos (“great, violent”).
gross.g: Remarkably great, big, vast in an often unpleasant way; (of behaviour) Highly or conspicuously offensive.

ground.g: Crushed, or reduced to small particles.

grounded.e: From Middle English grounded, i-grounded, equivalent to ground + -ed.

grounds.e: From ground, past participle of to grind.
grounds.g: The sediment at the bottom of a liquid, or from which a liquid has been filtered.

group.e: From French groupe (“cluster, group”), from Italian gruppo, groppo (“a knot, heap, group, bag (of money)”). In the "group theory" sense, calqued from French groupe, a term coined by the young French mathematician Évariste Galois in 1830. Old English cropp, croppa (“cluster, bunch, sprout, flower, berry, ear of corn, crop”) (whence English crop).
group.g: A number of things or persons being in some relation to one another.

grove.e: From Middle English grove, grave, from Old English grāf, grāfa (“grove; copse”), from Proto-West Germanic *graib, *graibō (“branch, group of branches, thicket”), from Proto-Germanic *graibaz, *graibô (“branch, fork”).

grow.e: From Middle English growen, from Old English grōwan (“to grow, increase, flourish, germinate”), from Proto-West Germanic *grōan, from Proto-Germanic *grōaną (“to grow, grow green”), from Proto-Indo-European *gʰreh₁- (“to grow, become green”).
grow.g: To become larger, to increase in magnitude.

growl.e: From Middle English groulen, grollen, gurlen (“of the bowels: to growl, rumble”), either possibly from Old French groler (variant of croler (“to be agitated, shake”)), grouler, grouller (“to growl, grumble”), from Frankish *grullen, *gruljan or from Old English gryllan, both from Proto-Germanic *gruljaną (“to make a sound; to growl, grumble, rumble”).
growl.g: A deep, rumbling, threatening sound made in the throat by an animal.

grown.e: From Middle English growen. Morphologically grow + -n.

growth.g: An increase in size, number, value, or strength.

grudge.e: A variant of grutch (mid 15th-century, younger than begrudge), from Middle English grucchen (“to murmur, complain, feel envy, begrudge”), from Old French grouchier, groucier (“to murmur, grumble”), of Germanic origin, probably ultimately imitative.
grudge.g: Deep-seated and/or long-term animosity or ill will about something or someone, especially due to perceived mistreatment.

grumble.e: Probably from Middle French grommeler, from Old French grumeler (“to murmur, grumble”), from Middle Dutch *grommelen ("to murmur, mutter, grunt"; > Modern Dutch grommelen (“to grumble”)), frequentative of Middle Dutch grommen (“to growl, grunt”).
grumble.g: A high thundering, rumbling or growling sound.

grumbler.g: A person who persistently grumbles; a complainer.
